tagline.text: The gateway to Kalanggaman Island, an old port town on Leyte's west coast

location.label: Location
location.text: Northwestern coast of Leyte Island, a port municipality facing the Camotes Sea

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500~4,000 (per person, 1 night 2 days, based on a van from Ormoc, shared boat, entrance fees, lodging and meals)

children.text: Palompon is a first-class municipality on the northwestern coast of Leyte facing the Camotes Sea, and the port town where boats to Kalanggaman Island depart. In a day or two you can see St. Francis Xavier Church, which became an independent parish in 1784, the mangrove islet of Tabuk and the Masaba Falls river trek.

Palompon is an urban municipality on the northwestern coast of Leyte Island, with the Camotes Sea right off its shore. According to Wikipedia its area is 126.07 square kilometers, and the 2024 census counted 59,486 residents. It is divided into 50 barangays, ten of which are poblacion (town center) barangays. The land rises from sea level to as high as 535 m, so mountains stand behind the coastal town like a folding screen. The local language is Cebuano (the Kana dialect), with some Waray mixed in. Most travelers know Palompon as the town you pass through to reach Kalanggaman Island, but the town itself has a boat landing, an old church, a mangrove islet and a waterfall trek, enough to fill a relaxed day.

Its history goes back to around 1620. The settlement was first called Hinablayan, and the name is said to have changed through Palompong and Palumpun to the present Palompon. A local legend says the name comes from a cluster of mangrove seedlings, and that those seedlings piled up to form Tabuk Island. In 1737 the Jesuits built the first chapel, but it was burned in a raid by Muslim (Moro) pirates and was later rebuilt as a fortified refuge and church. In the late 17th century the town fought off Moro raiders in a nine-day battle, and a cannon in the plaza in front of the town hall is said to be a relic of that fight. On November 12, 1784 Palompon separated from neighboring Hilongos to become an independent parish, and in 1957 five barrios split off to form the town of Matag-ob.

The heart of a visit is St. Francis Xavier Church. Wikipedia explains that the present stone church was begun by the Jesuits and continued by the Augustinians, and describes it as the oldest church in Leyte. Several travel guides give 1784 as the founding year and say construction took 44 years. The claim of "oldest church" varies between guides, which sometimes say "one of the oldest churches in Leyte", so it is wiser not to state it as certain. The church has been renovated many times, but its original walls remain, and the ceiling murals are said to be worth seeing. The plaza around the church is small and easy to cover on foot, so a good plan is to see the church and plaza in the morning and head out to sea in the afternoon.
There are also sights by the sea and in the hills. Tabuk Marine Park and Bird Sanctuary is a mangrove islet about
10 minutes

by boat from town, said to have been declared a marine park and bird sanctuary in 1995. Giant fruit bats and many birds are reported to nest in the mangrove forest, and a lighthouse viewpoint looks down over it. Masaba Falls is a river trek along a waterfall that cascades in seven tiers, and Lantaw Palompon is known only as a viewpoint and rest area overlooking the town. The Tres Marias islets have also been featured in a Philippine newspaper as an eco-tourism destination, and a community-based eco-tourism and coastal resource management program has received an award, which suggests the town has long put effort into ecotourism. Kalanggaman Island is covered in its own entry, so here we focus on how to get a boat from Palompon.

This stone church has been extended and repaired over many years since it became an independent parish in 1784. The ceiling murals and original walls remain. Visit quietly during Mass and follow the instructions about photography inside.

blocks.title: The cannon in the town plaza

children.text: A cannon in the plaza is said to be a relic of the nine-day battle against Moro pirates in the late 17th century. It is a few minutes' walk from the church, so seeing both together makes the town's history easier to understand.

by boat from town. It was designated a sanctuary in 1995, and fruit bat and bird watching and a lighthouse view are mentioned. Ask the tourism office about how to visit and the fees.
A stream trek that follows a waterfall in seven tiers. The water rises in the rainy season and becomes dangerous, so go in the dry season with a guide. Check access and entrance fees locally.

This is described as a viewpoint overlooking the town and the sea. Little detail is available on its location and conditions of use, so it is best to ask the Eco-Tourism Office for directions.
Around the landing you can watch fishing boats and boats coming and going. It is a pleasant place to walk at dusk as the sun sets over the Camotes Sea.
Take a van to Palompon from the Ormoc bus terminal. It takes about 1.5 to 2 hours.

Have lunch on the island and stroll the sandbar. Bring your own water and food.
Take the boat back to Palompon and drop your bags at your lodging.
Watch the sunset on the shore and have dinner at a restaurant in town.
For a day trip you must take the first van from Ormoc. Check the time of the last van in advance, since it may leave early.
See St. Francis Xavier Church and the cannon in the plaza in front of the town hall.

Have lunch in town and rest.
Go on the Masaba Falls river trek, setting out with a local guide.
Return to your lodging and rest.
There is little information on Tabuk Island and Masaba Falls. Get the latest guidance at the Eco-Tourism Office before you go.
The most common way is to fly from Manila to Tacloban (TAC) and continue overland. Check flight schedules on the airline's website.
Air-conditioned vans to Palompon leave from the Tacloban New Bus Terminal (Barangay Abucay) and are said to take about 3.5 to 4 hours.
You can also reach Ormoc from another city such as Cebu and take a van from there.

items.title: Getting around town and to the islands

children.text: You can walk from the terminal to the Eco-Tourism Office.
For Kalanggaman Island or Tabuk Island you hire a boat. Boats are booked through the Eco-Tourism Office.
The dry season from November to May is the best time to visit Palompon. For trips to Kalanggaman Island, which require going out to sea, the dry season, weekdays and early mornings are recommended.
According to modeled climate data, annual rainfall is about 1,598 mm, with February the driest month and June to October the wettest. Average daily highs are 28–30°C and lows are 22–25°C.

Palompon has small and mid-sized lodgings and guesthouses, but information is limited, so check prices and facilities locally. Kalanggaman Island has no hotels, only simple options such as tents, cottages and a tipi house. A 2025 guide lists a tipi house room for two with breakfast at
, but check the location and availability.

Palompon is classed as a first-class municipality, and the town has higher-education institutions such as the Palompon Institute of Technology and Northern Leyte College. As a college town it has a fairly good supply of restaurants, shops and a market, and electricity is supplied by the LEYECO 5 cooperative. Simple supplies you need in town are available at the market and shops, but buy plenty of drinking water and snacks before heading to the island. The local area code is 053 and the postal code is 6538.

There are almost no shops on the island, so bring your own water and food. There is no fresh water or electricity, so bring a power bank and cash too. Restaurants in town serve Filipino home cooking and seafood, but for specific places it is safer to check recent reviews.
Book the boat to Kalanggaman Island and register for entry through the Eco-Tourism Office. The number given in a 2025 guide is (053) 555 9731, and it may change.
There is no fresh water or electricity on the island. Bring enough drinking water, food and a power bank.
Bring plenty of cash. Entrance fees and the boat must be paid in cash, and there are reportedly no ATMs nearby.
The sandbar appears and disappears with the tide. Check the tide table when planning.
Taking the first van from Ormoc makes a day trip to the island possible, but be sure to check the time of the last van.
Avoid Mass times at the church and dress modestly.
Entrance fees differ between guides, so it is safest to confirm the current rate at the office.
Boats may stop running in bad sea conditions. Leave some slack in your schedule when booking.
During heavy rain, stream treks such as Masaba Falls are dangerous.
Carry all your trash off the island. Follow the environmental rules and the limits on alcohol and loud music.
Do not camp outside the designated areas.
Check the latest notices for prices and operating information. The prices in this entry are based on 2025–2026 guides.
